match.reason: The bank's tree cards teach trees and their edge counts but never define a spanning tree as one that includes every vertex of a graph, so the new point adds an idea none of them covers.

draft.title: Trees and spanning trees
card: Tree
a connected graph with no cycles. A cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating an edge.
Edges
a tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges. A tree with 6 vertices has 5 edges.
Spanning tree
a tree made from some of the edges of a connected graph. It reaches every vertex of that graph.
Example
A connected graph has 5 vertices and 7 edges. Any spanning tree of it has 4 edges, so 7 − 4 = 3 edges must be left out to break every cycle.
draft.remember: A tree is connected with no cycles, and it has one fewer edge than vertices.

a.q: Mia draws a connected graph with no cycles on 12 vertices. How many edges does her graph have?
a.why: A connected graph with no cycles is a tree, and a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges, so 12 − 1 = 11. The answer 12 is tempting, but 12 edges on 12 vertices would force a cycle.
a.clue: No cycles and connected means it is a tree.

b.q: A connected graph has 8 vertices and 11 edges. How many edges must be removed to leave a spanning tree?
b.why: A spanning tree reaches all 8 vertices, so it has 8 − 1 = 7 edges. Edges removed = 11 − 7 = 4. The answer 3 comes from taking 11 − 8, which forgets that a tree has one fewer edge than vertices.
b.clue: First find how many edges the spanning tree keeps.

problems.detail: The card defines a cycle as 'a path that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating an edge.' In VCE terms, that describes a circuit (a closed trail). A cycle is a closed walk with no repeated vertices other than the start and end. Also, by the VCE definition a path cannot start and end at the same vertex. Suggested fix: 'a walk that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating any other vertex or any edge.'

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are correct, with answers 11 and 4. The card's definition of a cycle actually describes a circuit and misuses 'path' by VCE definitions, so it should be reworded.
